power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Dynamic structural equation modeling (DSEM) has become a central tool for analyzing intensive longitudinal data, such as data from ecological momentary assessment and daily diary studies.

In practice, DSEM is almost exclusively estimated in Mplus, a commercial, closed-source program, while packages built on the open-source probabilistic programming language Stan offer only a fixed selection of models.
This tutorial shows applied researchers how to implement DSEM directly in Stan.

Starting from a bivariate multilevel cross-lagged model with random effects, we build the model in three steps: a minimal working version, a non-centered reparameterization that resolves the convergence problems of the first version, and an extension that treats missing observations as parameters to be estimated.
Along the way, we explain how to read Stan's convergence and sampler diagnostics, how to inspect the results visually, and how to report a Bayesian DSEM.
On simulated data with known parameter values, the Stan implementation recovers the true values and closely reproduces the estimates of Mplus and of the R package mlts.

We then demonstrate the flexibility of working in Stan with two extensions that require only local changes to the code: residual DSEM, and a binary within-person predictor, illustrated with data from a micro-randomized mindfulness intervention.
All code is openly available and written to be adapted to new models.

Working directly in Stan requires more initial effort than Mplus, but it makes every modeling decision transparent and extensible, and it lets researchers fit the model their research question calls for.
Dynamic Structural Equation Modeling (DSEM) is a statistical framework used to model the relations among multiple time-varying latent and observed variables.
It combines time-series modeling, structural equation modeling, and multilevel modeling (Hamaker et al., 2023).
text.formatted: It combines time-series modeling, structural equation modeling, and multilevel modeling <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Hamaker et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: DSEM is particularly useful in fields where researchers are interested in investigating intensive longitudinal data such as psychology, epidemiology, and economics.

The need for DSEM is in part a response to the technological innovations and availability of smart devices that have made data collection through daily diaries, ambulatory assessment, and ecological momentary assessment more easily accessible and feasible (McNeish & Hamaker, 2020).
text.formatted: The need for DSEM is in part a response to the technological innovations and availability of smart devices that have made data collection through daily diaries, ambulatory assessment, and ecological momentary assessment more easily accessible and feasible <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(McNeish & Hamaker, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: These methods afford researchers to collect longitudinal data across a larger number of subjects, with more frequent and a larger number of time-points.
On a conceptual level, intensive longitudinal data allow researchers to capture within-person processes as they unfold over time in individuals' everyday lives.
This has been recognized as a key advantage in multiple areas of psychological research and has contributed to a growing community of researchers applying these methods.

For instance, DSEM has been employed to investigate the reciprocal relationship between negative affect and rumination (Blanke et al., 2020), as well as the interplay between parent-adolescent interactions and parental well-being (Bülow et al., 2022).

text.text: Emerging applications of DSEM also include its use in cognitive-behavioral tasks and reaction time data to capture momentary fluctuations in cognitive performance, such as in children with ADHD (Aristodemou et al., 2024).

text.text: It has also been used to link cognitive control to the dynamics of emotion regulation in adolescents' daily lives (Debra et al., 2024).

text.text: Mplus offers researchers the lowest practical barrier to entry: its DSEM module is well documented, actively developed, and automatically handles many practical complications, such as unequally spaced measurement occasions and latent centering.
This convenience comes with some constraints.
Mplus requires a paid license, which can be a barrier for students, early-career researchers, and institutions with limited funding.
It is closed-source, so users have limited insight into its internal computations, default settings, and estimation procedures, which makes it harder to reproduce, audit, or extend an analysis.

Its input format also imposes practical restrictions: data must be supplied as a plain-text file whose records may not exceed 10,000 characters, and variables with a variance above 1,000,000 are rejected and must first be rescaled (Muthén & Muthén, 1998 -2017).

text.text: Finally, Mplus offers fewer convergence diagnostics than, for example, Stan (see below) (Muthén & Muthén, n.d.).

text.text: Stan (Stan Development Team, 2025) is an open-source probabilistic programming language for Bayesian inference.
text.formatted: Stan <ref type="bibr">(Stan Development Team, 2025</ref>) is an open-source probabilistic programming language for Bayesian inference.

text.text: Rather than offering a menu of predefined models, Stan lets users write down their model directly: any model that can be expressed as a probabilistic generative model can, in principle, be implemented.

Once the logic of a DSEM is written out in Stan code, extending it (for example with additional predictors, other outcome distributions, or a new measurement model) becomes a matter of adding or adapting a few lines rather than waiting for a software update.
In addition, Stan has several practical advantages.
It is freely available and fully open-source.
Every modeling choice is visible in the code and can be inspected, questioned, changed, and shared.

It integrates with statistical environments like R and Python, enabling highly customizable visualizations through packages such as ggplot2 (Wickham, 2016) and bayesplot (Gabry & Mahr, 2025) in R or matplotlib (Hunter, 2007) in Python.
text.formatted: It integrates with statistical environments like R and Python, enabling highly customizable visualizations through packages such as ggplot2 <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(Wickham, 2016)</ref> and bayesplot <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Gabry & Mahr, 2025)</ref> in R or matplotlib <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Hunter, 2007)</ref> in Python.

text.text: Its Hamiltonian Monte Carlo sampler uses information from the model to take bigger, better-guided steps to explore many parameters simultaneously, whereas a Gibbs sampler (used by, for example, Mplus) changes only one or a few parameters at a time, which can require many more iterations, and thus more time, to explore the posterior.
Furthermore, Stan by default warns users when something may be wrong, not only with convergence but also with the posterior samples.

Specifically, Stan warns about (1) divergent transitions, which indicate difficulties in exploring some areas of the posterior distribution and suggest potential issues with model specification; (2) low effective sample size (ESS), indicating that the posterior samples are highly correlated and may not sufficiently represent the posterior distribution; (3) reaching the maximum treedepth, meaning the sampler may have stopped early; and (4) low Bayesian fraction of missing information (BFMI), suggesting inefficiencies in the sampler's momentum.
Stan also suggests how to address these warnings and gives direct control over the sampler settings.
Together, these diagnostics provide a more comprehensive picture of whether the posterior samples can be trusted (Betancourt, 2018).
text.formatted: Together, these diagnostics provide a more comprehensive picture of whether the posterior samples can be trusted <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Betancourt, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Several R packages make Stan accessible without writing Stan code. brms (Bürkner, 2017) is an excellent interface for a wide range of generalized linear multilevel models and can accommodate certain autoregressive designs, but it does not provide a dedicated framework for DSEM. ctsem (Driver & Voelkle, 2018) focuses on dynamic models, but in continuous rather than discrete time.

text.text: Most relevant here is the mlts package (Koslowski et al., 2025), which uses precompiled Stan models to fit a selection of multilevel latent time series models through simple R functions.

text.text: It supports manifest and latent VAR models with measurement models, between-level covariates, and multi-group comparisons, and provides tools for model checking and presentation, including automatic L A T E X model equations, path diagrams, and posterior predictive checks via bayesplot (Gabry & Mahr, 2025).

text.text: There is a clear place for these packages.

For researchers whose model falls within their scope, they are free and benefit from Stan's sampler and diagnostics, and require minimal programming effort; they are also a valuable sanity check for a custom implementation.

Their convenience, however, comes from fixing the model in advance: because mlts relies on precompiled models, users cannot modify the underlying code, and at the time of writing categorical variables and residual DSEM models are not yet supported.
This tutorial is written for researchers who do not want to be limited by what a package currently supports, or who want full transparency over how their model is estimated.

A tutorial is needed because Stan's flexibility is locked behind a learning curve: Stan requires users to write the entire model in a probabilistic programming language, which can be a barrier for those with limited coding experience.
With this tutorial paper we hope to flatten this learning curve.
We begin by introducing a base bivariate DSEM commonly used in psychological research and then walk through the process of implementing this model in Stan.
The modeling process unfolds in three steps: First, we present the simplest version of the model, containing only the essential code required for the model to run.
Next, we reparameterize the model to improve sampling efficiency and model convergence.
In a third and final step, we extend the model to handle missing data.
After the base model is built, we show how to respecify it as a residual DSEM and then extend the model to handle categorical predictors.
Along the way we teach how to evaluate convergence, present results visually, and compare the output from Stan and Mplus across these models to discuss the implications and limitations.
The Stan code and modeling skills presented here are intentionally general and modular, so that readers can adapt the models to their own needs after the tutorial.
Intended audience and prerequisites.

We assume familiarity with the core concepts of DSEM, such as the within/between decomposition, autoregressive and cross-lagged effects, and random effects (Hamaker et al., 2023; McNeish & Hamaker, 2020), with the basics of Bayesian estimation (priors, posteriors, and MCMC; McElreath, 2020), and with basic R. No prior Stan programming experience is required.

In the VARIABLE block, NAMES = subject observation X Y; specifies the variable names, while CLUSTER = subject; identifies the subject-level clustering required for multilevel modeling.

We will start with the simplest implementation of the model and discuss potential convergence problems that might occur in this formulation.
We will then resolve those problems through reparameterization, an important tool for modeling in Stan.
We chose this multi-step approach to highlight strategies to deal with issues of model convergence.
Finally, building upon the reparameterized model, we demonstrate how to account for missing data.

In our Stan model, the first segment we need to define is the data block.
This block specifies the structure and type of data the model is passed by the user (see above).
Following the above example, we have gathered data from N subj subjects, each providing N obs measurements.
We assume the measurements are taken at constant intervals, such as once daily.
The most effective way to structure this data is in a matrix format, with dimensions N subj × N obs for each variable of interest.

Here, we simply declare them so that they are available for use.
In our model, we specify the fixed-effect parameters γ 1 through γ 8 and the individual-level random effects u i1 through u i8 from Equation 3, and the covariance matrix Ω from Equation 4.
Estimating the covariance matrix directly can be challenging because it must meet certain mathematical criteria (i.e., symmetry and positive definiteness).

To ensure meeting these criteria, Stan recommends using a technique called Cholesky decomposition (Stan Development Team, 2022), which is conceptually similar to factoring a covariance matrix into simpler components: the lower triangular correlation matrix (as opposed to the entire matrix) and standard deviations of each random effect parameter.

Together with the fixed and random effects parameters, we declare the decomposed covariance matrix parameters with the following Stan code: Code 3: Stan parameters block (2_simple.stan) parameters { vector [8] gamma ; // fixed effects array [ N_subj ] vector [8] u ; // random effects // Components for covariance matrix of random effects cholesk y _ f a c t o r _ c o r r [8] L_Omega ; // lower triangular corr . matrix vector < lower =0 >[8] tau_Omega ; // standard deviations }

The disadvantage is that every occurrence of 8 must be updated when parameters are added or removed, as in the categorical model in the Extension: Categorical Predictor Variables section.
In applications, we recommend declaring the number of random effects as data (e.g., int<lower=1> K;) and using K throughout.

text.text: We reconstruct the full correlation matrix R_Omega and covariance matrix Omega from the Cholesky decomposition components in the transformed parameters block (See Code 4).
The first two lines declare the final correlation and covariance matrices.

The next two lines compute these matrices (R_Omega is derived by multiplying the Cholesky factor with its transpose, and Omega is obtained by scaling the correlation matrix with the standard deviations).
Performing these calculations in the transformed parameters block, rather than the parameters block, ensures that the resulting matrices are stored and readily accessible after estimation.

Code 4: Stan transformed parameters block (2_simple.stan) transformed parameters { corr_matrix [8] R_Omega ; // correlation matrix ( random effects ) cov_matrix [8] Omega ; // covariance matrix ( random effects ) R_Omega = m u l t i p l y _ l o w e r _ t r i _ s e l f _ t r a n s p o s e ( L_Omega ); Omega = quad_form_diag ( R_Omega , tau_Omega ); } The model Block
The model block generally houses two main building parts of our model: The specification of the priors and the specification of the model equations.
While Mplus has default priors behind the scenes, Stan requires their explicit specification.
We begin the model block by specifying priors for our three groups of parameters.
The three priors chosen here (Normal, Cauchy, and LKJ) are commonly used and generally suitable for DSEM applications.

Like the Mplus defaults, which place (near-)flat Normal priors on coefficients and inverse-Gamma and inverse-Wishart priors on (co)variances (Asparouhov & Muthén, 2010), they are broad and only weakly informative.
text.formatted: Like the Mplus defaults, which place (near-)flat Normal priors on coefficients and inverse-Gamma and inverse-Wishart priors on (co)variances <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Asparouhov & Muthén, 2010)</ref>, they are broad and only weakly informative.

text.text: As a starting point, the gamma ∼ normal(0, 100); prior sets a diffuse Normal prior on the fixed effects, reflecting uncertainty and allowing values to vary widely.

The prior tau_Omega ∼ cauchy(0, 2.5); is a weakly informative half-Cauchy prior for standard deviations (the lower bound of zero on tau_Omega truncates the Cauchy), often recommended in hierarchical models because it allows for a wide range of variability while still gently discouraging extreme values (Gelman, 2006).

text.text: The L_Omega ∼ lkj_corr_cholesky(1.0); pairs naturally with the Cholesky decomposition approach introduced in the previous block.
In using Cholesky decomposition, the lower triangular correlation matrix is the only part that needs a prior.
The shape parameter of 1.0 corresponds to a uniform prior over all valid correlation matrices, meaning it does not favor any particular correlation structure (Lewandowski et al., 2009).

text.text: These priors are a starting point rather than a recommendation for every application.

Because Stan, unlike Mplus, requires all priors to be stated explicitly, researchers should choose them deliberately and scale them to the parameter they govern: an autoregressive coefficient, a person mean, and a log residual variance live on very different scales, and a single diffuse prior is rarely weakly informative for all of them.
Priors matter most for weakly identified parameters, such as small random-effect variances, where the data carry little information.

We therefore recommend visualizing the priors (e.g., through prior predictive checks) and reporting a sensitivity analysis showing that substantive conclusions are stable across a defensible range of priors (Depaoli & van de Schoot, 2017; Schubert et al., 2025).

In the likelihood portion of the model block (See Code 6), we specify how the observed data are generated according to our model assumptions.
The code first loops over each subject to define their unique set of parameters.
Specifically, the individual-level fixed effects (gamma) and random effects (u i ) combine to determine subject-specific parameter values.
These calculations follow the model equations verbatim (See Equations 3).
We use the Stan data type real for these parameters because they represent single numeric values rather than vectors or matrices.
Each individual's vector of random effects u i is assumed to follow a multivariate normal distribution with mean zero and covariance matrix.
Next, we calculate within-person deviations (X_w, Y_w) by subtracting latent individual-level means from observed values (i.e., latent person-mean centering).

Finally, we define the within-level likelihood, which loops over each observation from the second occasion onwards (see below) and directly reflects the DSEM equations introduced previously (see Equations 2): autoregressive terms, cross-lagged regression effects, and residual variances are explicitly modeled.

( see above ) // likelihood for ( i in 1: N_subj ) { // random effects follow multivariate normal // with mean 0 and covariance matrix Omega u [ i ] ∼ multi_normal ( rep_vector (0 , 8) , Omega ); // obtain individual means and regression parameters real mu_X = gamma [1] + u [i ,1]; real mu_Y = gamma [2] + u [i ,2]; real phi_X = gamma [3] + u [i ,3]; real phi_Y = gamma [4] + u [i ,4]; real beta_X = gamma [5] + u [i ,5]; real beta_Y = gamma [6] + u [i ,6]; real psi_X = sqrt ( exp ( gamma [7] + u [i ,7])); real psi_Y = sqrt ( exp ( gamma [8] + u [i ,8])); // person -mean centering observed values vector [ N_obs ] X_w = X [ i ] -mu_X ; vector [ N_obs ] Y_w = Y [ i ] -mu_Y ; for ( t in 2: N_obs ) { // within -level model X_w [ t ]∼normal ( phi_X * X_w [t -1] + beta_X * Y_w [t -1] , psi_X ); Y_w [ t ]∼normal ( phi_Y * Y_w [t -1] + beta_Y * X_w [ t ] , psi_Y ); } } }
The within-level loop starts at t = 2 so that the lagged predictors at t -1 are defined; starting at t = 1 would reference a non-existent occasion 0.
As a consequence, the first observation of each person enters the model only as a lagged predictor and not as an outcome.
This is known as the initial conditions problem, and we take this approach for simplicity.
Alternatives exist: Mplus, for example, treats the unobserved values before the first occasion as missing data and imputes them during estimation (Asparouhov et al., 2018).

text.text: The ˆ︁ R (Rhat) statistic assesses convergence by comparing the variance within chains to the variance between chains.
Values close to 1.0 indicate that the chains have likely converged to the same posterior distribution.
Following the latest guidance from Vehtari et al. (2021), it is advisable to consider the sample to be reliable only if all ˆ︁ R values fall below 1.01 with a minimum of four chains.
Specifically, running fewer than four chains increases the risk of failing to detect non-convergence issues, and using a ˆ︁ R threshold as high as 1.05 may prematurely signal convergence.

The default in Mplus executes only two MCMC chains and utilizes a convergence diagnostic known as the Potential Scale Reduction Factor (PSRF), equivalent to the ˆ︁ R statistic, with a cut-off value of 1.05.
The second diagnostic, Effective Sample Size (ESS), reflects how much independent information is contained in the posterior samples.
If a chain produces highly autocorrelated draws, then the number of effectively independent samples is much lower than the total number of iterations.
The bulk ESS assesses sampling efficiency in the high-density region of the posterior, while the tail ESS evaluates the adequacy of sampling in the extreme(s).
According to Vehtari et al. (2021), both bulk and tail ESS should exceed 400 to ensure stable and reliable estimates.

Moreover, they recommend that each split chain achieves an average ESS of at least 50 for the ˆ︁ R statistic to be a meaningful convergence diagnostic, making a minimum of four chains essential for robust inference.
In Stan, ESS is a default measure of convergence.
Mplus did not have the option to access ESS statistics until, and only in, version 9 (released October 2025).
This limits the user's ability to evaluate the reliability of the estimates even if the ˆ︁ R falls below the cutoff of 1.01 Zitzmann et al.
Stan did not report any warnings or convergence issues during the sampling of our simple base model.
Nonetheless, it is good practice to inspect the sampler diagnostics explicitly.

This can be done by running the final command in Code 8, which returns three key metrics: (1) the number of divergent transitions, (2) the number of iterations that hit the maximum tree depth, and (3) the estimated Bayesian fraction of missing information (E-BFMI) for each chain (Figure 1D).

text.text: A divergent transition indicates that the sampler had difficulty exploring a region of the posterior distribution; zero divergences suggest that the model was well-behaved throughout sampling.

A maximum treedepth hit means that the sampler reached its limit for how far it can explore in a single iteration before being satisfied with its reached value; in our simple base model run, no iterations needed the full maximum treedepth.
Finally, E-BFMI is a measure of sampler efficiency; values above 0.3 are generally considered acceptable (Betancourt, 2016 (Betancourt, , 2018)).

In such a case, there is a general recommendation to increase the number of sampling iterations and re-run the model.
However, there are faster and well-established strategies to improve convergence in Stan.
One widely recommended approach is reparameterizing the model, which can resolve elevated ˆ︁ R values, low ESS values, and divergent transitions more reliably (Stan Development Team, 2025).

text.text: Simply put, reparameterization alters the parameterization of the model to facilitate smoother exploration by the sampler resulting in better convergence.
We will discuss implementing this strategy in the next section, followed by an elaboration on treatment of missing values.

These two sections will equip researchers with the tools needed to deal with real-world issues (convergence issues in complex models, missing data due to non-perfect compliance) they will likely encounter when applying these models to empirical data.
In the simple formulation, each subject's random-effect vector u i is drawn directly from a multivariate normal:
When Ω induces strong correlations, sampling u i can be slow or lead to divergent transitions.

To let the sampler explore the posterior faster and avoid divergent transitions, we switch to a reparameterized (also known as non-centered) form (Betancourt & Girolami, 2015; Papaspiliopoulos et al., 2007).

text.text: To do so, we introduce latent standard-normal variables α u,i ∼ N (0, I), where I is the identity matrix, ensuring each component of α u,i is independent and normally distributed.
We then recover u i by "stretching and rotating" α u,i using the Cholesky factor of Ω.
Concretely, if Ω = L Ω L ⊤ Ω ,
Because α u,i is uncorrelated by construction, this often lets the sampler explore the posterior faster, that is, it yields more effective samples per unit of computation time.
It is important to note that this reparameterization is a purely mathematical trick: it does not change the model.
Because α u,i is standard normal, L Ω α u,i has mean 0 and covariance L Ω I L ⊤ Ω = Ω, so u i follows exactly the same N (0, Ω) distribution as before.
What changes is only which quantities the sampler works with: the sampler explores the Why does this help?
The difficulty lies in the posterior geometry, that is, the shape of the posterior distribution in parameter space.

In the centered parameterization, the plausible values of u i depend strongly on the random-effect standard deviations: when a standard deviation is small, the corresponding u i are squeezed close to zero, and when it is large, they spread out.

This produces a funnel-shaped posterior that is hard to traverse with a single step size, which shows up as divergent transitions, low ESS, and (Betancourt & Girolami, 2015; Papaspiliopoulos et al., 2007).

text.text: In the non-centered parameterization, the α u,i are a priori independent of the standard deviations, which largely removes this funnel.

Consistent with recommendations by Lüdtke, Robitzsch, and Grund (Grund et al., 2018 (Grund et al., , 2021;; Lüdtke et al., 2017), we handle missingness under MAR by treating each missing entry as an unknown parameter and sampling it from the posterior predictive distribution conditional on the multilevel/DSEM structure.

text.text: This substantive-model-compatible strategy makes the imputation model at least as general as the analysis model, preserving within-between decompositions, random slopes, and cross-level interactions.

Prior work shows that single-level imputation can bias regression parameters and variance components in clustered data, and that special care is needed when imputing predictors with random slopes (Enders et al., 2016; Grund et al., 2016); our Stan specification builds the multilevel (and dynamic) structure directly into the likelihood to avoid these issues.

text.text: In the data block, we now provide Stan with the locations of missing values and how many there are.
Then, in the parameters block, we add X_mis and Y_mis, which are simply new parameters representing the unknown (missing) observations.
The main logic is implemented in the transformed parameters block, where we create two new arrays, X_imp and Y_imp, which start as copies of the observed data.
We then overwrite the missing entries in those arrays with their corresponding estimated values.
The priors on the missing values are hard-coded in the model block.
We center them on the grand means of the simulated data (3 for X and 1 for Y ; see Table 3) and give them a standard deviation of 10, which is wide relative to the scale of the data.
text.formatted: We center them on the grand means of the simulated data (3 for X and 1 for Y ; see Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_2">3</ref>) and give them a standard deviation of 10, which is wide relative to the scale of the data.

text.text: In applied work, these values should be chosen to reflect the measurement scale, for example, centered on the observed sample mean with a standard deviation that comfortably covers the response range.

Because each missing value also enters the likelihood as an outcome and as a lagged predictor, its posterior is informed mainly by the person's surrounding observations and the dynamic structure of the model, so the prior plays a minor role as long as it is not overly narrow or placed far from the plausible range.
This design allows us to reuse the rest of the model almost without modification.

The likelihood calculations are identical to the previous model, except they now operate on X_imp and Y_imp instead of the original X and Y. Stan will jointly estimate the fixed effects, random effects, and missing data values, using both prior information and the observed data.

This results in full posterior distributions for every quantity of interest, including the missing values, while automatically accounting for their uncertainty (Gelman et al., 2013; Lüdtke et al., 2017).

Bayesian DSEM involves more analytic decisions than a typical frequentist multilevel model, and many of them are invisible in the final parameter table: the choice and scale of the priors, the parameterization of the random-effect covariance matrix, the treatment of missing observations, and the sampler settings all shape the posterior.
Transparent reporting of these choices is therefore not a formality but a precondition for replication and for readers to judge whether the posterior can be trusted.
Four chains were run for 1000 warm-up and 2000 post-warm-up iterations each, yielding 8000 retained draws without thinning (seed = 2026).

text.text: The function mlts_model() specifies the model structure: q = 2 declares two time-varying constructs, max_lag = 1 sets first-order autoregressive and cross-lagged effects, and incl_t0_effects = "phi(0)_21" adds the contemporaneous (lag-0) directed path from X to Y , matching the β Y parameter in Equation 2.

Because mlts_model() includes the full lag-1 matrix by default, i.e., both cross-lagged effects, fixef_zero = "phi(1)_21" constrains the effect of X t-1 on Y t (and its random effect variance) to zero, so that the model contains the same within-level paths as our Stan model.
Setting inno_covs_zero = TRUE constrains the innovation covariance to zero, consistent with our Stan specification.
By default, all autoregressive effects, cross-lagged effects, and log innovation variances are estimated as random effects, matching the between-level structure in Equations 3a-3h.
The function mlts_fit() then passes the model and data to a precompiled Stan model via rstan, and handles the internal data preparation automatically.

Note that mlts uses slightly different default priors than our Stan model: Normal(0, 10) for means and log innovation variances, Normal(0, 2) for dynamic parameters, and Cauchy(0, 2.5) for random effect standard deviations, compared to Normal(0, 100) for all fixed effects in our Stan specification.
With the sample sizes typical of ILD studies, these differences have negligible impact on the posterior estimates.

text.text: The fixed effect estimates are in close agreement across all three tools, confirming that our Stan implementation produces equivalent results.
The mlts run did, however, produce convergence warnings: 29 divergent transitions, a maximum ˆ︁ R of 1.037, and minimum bulk and tail effective sample sizes of 107 and 173, respectively.
These difficulties were concentrated in the small random effect variance components.

Specifically, the random effect standard deviations of the autoregressive effect of Y (0.12) and of the cross-lagged effect from Y t-1 to X t (0.16) had among the lowest effective sample sizes of the reported parameters, as such small variance components create a challenging posterior geometry for the sampler (Betancourt & Girolami, 2015).

The reparameterization approach demonstrated in this tutorial offers a complementary solution: rather than removing the random effect, the non-centered parameterization allows the sampler to explore the posterior efficiently even when variance components are small, preserving the full model structure.
The autoregressive parameters ϕ Xi and ϕ Y i quantify how strongly each variable at time t-1 predicts itself at time t.
In psychological research, these parameters reflect constructs like emotional inertia, which is the tendency for affective states to persist over time (Koval et al., 2012; Kuppens et al., 2010).
text.formatted: In psychological research, these parameters reflect constructs like emotional inertia, which is the tendency for affective states to persist over time <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Koval et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Kuppens et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: However, as Asparouhov and Muthén (2020) point out, the standard DSEM autoregressive coefficient does not capture pure inertia.

Because the lagged predictor X (w) it-1 includes variance that was already explained by a cross-lagged effect at time t-1, the autoregressive parameter conflates genuine carry-over with the re-prediction of variance that was already accounted for.
This can inflate estimates of inertia and complicate the interpretation of both autoregressive and cross-lagged effects.

The residual DSEM (RDSEM) framework (Asparouhov & Muthén, 2020; Asparouhov et al., 2018) addresses this by having the autoregressive process operate on residuals, that is, on what remains of a variable after its structural prediction has been removed.
text.formatted: The residual DSEM (RDSEM) framework <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Asparouhov & Muthén, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Asparouhov et al., 2018)</ref> addresses this by having the autoregressive process operate on residuals, that is, on what remains of a variable after its structural prediction has been removed.

text.text: In Asparouhov et al. (2018), this structural prediction is contemporaneous (lag-0), so that the AR process carries forward only what the concurrent cross-sectional model cannot explain.

In our bivariate cross-lagged model, however, the structural predictors follow the lag structure of Equation 2: X (w) it is structurally predicted by the lagged cross-lag β Xi Y (w) it-1 , and Y (w) it is predicted by the contemporaneous link β Y i X (w) it .
We adapt the RDSEM principle accordingly, so that the autoregressive effect of each variable carries forward only the portion that was not already explained by its respective structural predictor.
Note that this is only one of several defensible specifications.
Alternatively, the cross-lagged effect could be treated as part of the residual process, so that the residuals follow a full VAR(1) model including residual cross-lagged effects.
Which choice is appropriate depends on the substantive question; the point of the implementation below is that Stan can encode any of these assumptions by changing how the residuals are defined.
To formalize this, we define the within-person residuals at each occasion as the deviation from the structural prediction:

The RDSEM likelihood then replaces the raw lagged terms with these residuals in the autoregressive component, while the structural predictions remain unchanged: residuals, each loading on its observed within-person score with a weight fixed to 1.

(A) Standard DSEM: ϕ X and ϕ Y are autoregressive effects of the lagged within-person scores, β X is the cross-lagged effect of Y (w) t-1 on X (w) t , β Y is the contemporaneous effect of X (w) t on Y (w) t , and ψ X and ψ Y are the residual standard deviations.
The residuals are independent across occasions, so no path connects e (w) t-1 and e (w) t .

(B) Residual DSEM: the autoregressive effects connect the residuals rather than the observed scores, so that only the part of X (w) t-1 and Y (w) t-1 not explained by the structural predictors is carried forward (Equation 5); ψ X and ψ Y are now the standard deviations of the innovations of the residual processes.
The structural paths into X (w) t-1 and Y (w) t-1 (from occasion t -2) are omitted for clarity.
Black dots indicate parameters that vary across persons as random effects.
Comparing Equation 6 with the standard DSEM likelihood in Equation 2, the only difference is that ϕ Xi now multiplies e (w) Xit-1 instead of X (w) it-1 , and ϕ Y i multiplies e (w) it-1 .
The autoregressive parameters can now be interpreted as the carry-over of the unexplained part of each variable.
This distinction is substantively important whenever cross-lagged effects are non-trivial.

For example, in experience sampling studies of emotion regulation, accounting for time trends and concurrent predictors via RDSEM can change the magnitude and even the direction of estimated autoregressive effects, and that standard DSEM sometimes fails to converge in settings where RDSEM does (Debra et al., 2024).

text.text: A practical advantage of our Stan implementation is that the RDSEM extension requires no new parameters, no changes to the between-level structure, and no modifications to the missing data handling.
The only adaptation is in the within-level loop.
In the full model (Code 11), the two likelihood lines are replaced with four: two lines that compute the residuals, and two lines that use those residuals in the autoregressive component.
One indexing consequence follows directly from the lag structure of the model.
Because e (w) it-2 (that is, the residual of X at t-1 after removing the cross-lagged prediction from Y at t-2), the lagged residual e (w)
Xit-1 can only be formed from t = 3 onwards (the residual e (w) it-1 would already be available at t = 2).
The loop therefore starts at t = 3 rather than t = 2.

As a consequence, the first two occasions of each person enter the model only as lagged predictors and not as outcomes, one occasion more than in the standard DSEM (see the paragraph on initial conditions in the Implementation in Stan: Simplest Model section).

text.text: Compared to the full model, two things have changed: the loop starts at t = 3, and each likelihood statement now uses a residualized lag.
The residual X_resid is the value of X at t-1 minus its cross-lagged prediction from Y one occasion earlier (beta_X*Y_w[t-2]), so that phi_X acts only on the unexplained component.
Analogously, Y_resid is the value of Y at t-1 minus its contemporaneous prediction from X at that same occasion (beta_Y*X_w[t-1]).
All other parts of the model (the between-level covariance structure, random effects, missing data imputation, and priors) remain identical to Code 11.
The simplicity of the RDSEM implementation on top of the full model illustrates one of the key strengths of working directly in Stan.

While learning to write Stan code is not trivial, the investment yields considerable flexibility: researchers can add or remove model components to suit their specific research questions, without being constrained by the feature set of any particular software package.

text.text: Within-Person Model of the Categorical DSEM

In the models presented so far, all variables were continuous, and within-person centering was straightforward: the within-person deviation was simply the observed value minus the person-specific intercept.
A binary variable like MI requires a more complex solution.
Person-mean centering a 0/1 variable produces a continuous deviation score that conflates the between-person probability of receiving MI with the occasion-level deviation.

Moreover, the observed person mean is only an error-prone estimate of a person's true MI propensity (i.e., the person-specific probability of receiving the treatment, expressed on the probit scale). Lüdtke et al. (2008) showed that using such observed means in place of the true means yields biased estimates of between-person (contextual) effects, and that this bias is largest when the number of observations per person is small and the between-person variance is small relative to the within-person variance, that is, when the observed means are unreliable.

(2008)</ref> showed that using such observed means in place of the true means yields biased estimates of between-person (contextual) effects, and that this bias is largest when the number of observations per person is small and the between-person variance is small relative to the within-person variance, that is, when the observed means are unreliable.

text.text: In Mplus, this is handled via latent decomposition: behind each observed MI it lies a continuous latent variable MI * it , linked to the binary outcome through a probit model, which is decomposed into betweenand within-person components.

In Stan, rather than estimating MI * (w) it as an explicit parameter for every person-occasion combination (which would dramatically increase the number of parameters to be estimated), we implement this latent decomposition by analytically marginalizing MI * (w) it out of the likelihood.
That is, we use the mathematical structure of the model to account for all possible values of MI * (w) it without ever sampling it directly.
This is possible because MI * (w) it enters both the RU and NA equations linearly, and its prior is standard normal.

The product of normal densities is itself proportional to a normal density, so the integral over MI * (w) it has a closed form obtained by completing the square (Bishop, 2006); the probit constraint contributes a truncation factor in the spirit of the latent-variable formulation of binary-response models (Albert & Chib, 1993).

Two further details are handled inside the helper.

When MI is missing at an occasion, that occasion still contributes the information from RU and NA, so that their imputed values remain informed by the model; it simply carries no information about the threshold.

And for extreme values, the helper uses a numerically stable version of the normal cumulative distribution function, so that the sampler does not run into numbers too small for the computer to represent (see Appendix B).

As in the previous models, the loop starts at t = 2 because the lagged values of RU and NA are not defined at the first occasion (see the paragraph on initial conditions in the Implementation in Stan: Simplest Model section).

Stan and Mplus agree closely on every parameter: all differences in posterior means are small relative to the width of the credible intervals, and all R values are at or below 1.03.

The substantive conclusions are therefore identical across both implementations: the mindfulness intervention reduced both rumination (β M IRU : Stan = -2.35, Mplus = -2.36) and negative affect (β M IN A : Stan = -1.22, Mplus = -1.22), with credible intervals excluding zero in both cases.
The autoregressive effects also agree well (ϕ RU RU : Stan = 0.22, Mplus = 0.22; ϕ N AN A : Stan = 0.35, Mplus = 0.37).
The largest difference in absolute terms, for the grand mean of rumination (-0.42, on a scale where the credible intervals span roughly 8 points), is negligible in substantive terms.
The probit threshold is close to zero in both implementations, reflecting the roughly equal allocation of mindfulness and control occasions in the micro-randomized design.
We note that reaching this level of agreement required considerable effort.
Mplus is closed-source software, and not every detail of its estimation procedure is fully documented.

For example, the DSEM documentation states that the threshold of a binary variable may be replaced by a mean parameter "depending on the structural model at hand" (Asparouhov et al., 2018, p. 366), without specifying when, and the exact form of the default threshold prior is not clearly defined (Asparouhov & Muthén, 2010; Padgett et al., 2023).

Discussion This tutorial demonstrated how to implement Dynamic Structural Equation Models in Stan, starting from a minimal working model and building toward a fully reparameterized implementation with principled missing data handling.
We showed that Stan faithfully reproduces Mplus estimates on simulated data with known ground truth parameters, while offering greater transparency, flexibility, and diagnostic depth.

Beyond replicating a bivariate DSEM, we extended the model in two directions that are not currently available in mlts (Koslowski et al., 2025): residual DSEM (RDSEM), which separates genuine autoregressive carry-over from variance already explained by structural predictors, and categorical predictor variables handled via marginalization of the latent continuous variable.

The choice between Stan, Mplus, and mlts ultimately comes down to a three-way trade-off between accessibility, cost, and flexibility.

Mplus offers the lowest practical barrier to entry for researchers: the DSEM module is well-documented, actively developed, and handles many practical complications such as unequally spaced measurement occasions and latent centering automatically.
Several excellent tutorials for learning DSEM in Mplus have been published as well (Hamaker et al., 2023; McNeish & Hamaker, 2020; McNeish & MacKinnon, 2025; McNeish et al., 2024).

text.text: However, Mplus carries a substantial licensing cost that can be prohibitive for students, early-career researchers, and institutions.
It is also a closed blackbox system: researchers cannot inspect or modify the underlying estimation code, which limits both transparency and extensibility.
When a desired model feature is not yet implemented, the only option is to wait for a future software release.
The mlts package occupies a useful middle ground.
It is free, open-source, and builds on Stan's Hamiltonian Monte Carlo sampler, so it inherits Stan's diagnostic framework.

For models that fall within its current scope, including bivariate and multivariate VAR models with between-level covariates and optional measurement models, mlts requires minimal programming effort and produces results that closely match both Mplus and our Stan implementation.
An introduction to mlts for novice users is also available (Koslowski et al., 2025).
text.formatted: An introduction to mlts for novice users is also available <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Koslowski et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The ceiling of mlts is, however, fixed by its precompiled Stan models.
For example, RDSEM and categorical variables are not yet supported, and researchers cannot modify the underlying model code to add them.

As we showed in the comparison section, mlts can also encounter convergence difficulties in the centered parameterization when random effect variance components are near zero, a problem that the non-centered reparameterization demonstrated in this tutorial handles.
Writing Stan code directly requires the steepest initial investment, but the return on that investment is very high flexibility.

Any model that can be expressed as a probabilistic generative process can be implemented, and the modular structure of Stan code means that extensions such as the RDSEM and categorical models demonstrated here often require only localized changes to an existing model file.

For research groups that regularly push against the boundaries of available software, and that require full transparency and reproducibility in their estimation procedure, the learning curve is a one-time cost that might pay dividends across many future projects.
Mplus and our Stan implementation handle missing data in conceptually similar ways.

In Mplus, DSEM is estimated with a Gibbs sampler, and missing observations are imputed at each MCMC iteration conditional on the current parameter values and the neighboring observations (Asparouhov et al., 2018).

text.text: For the simulated dataset used in this tutorial, with 100 individuals and 50 observations each, total wall-clock time across four chains was approximately 244 seconds for the simple model, 342 seconds for the reparameterized model, and 600 seconds for the full model with 30% missing data, run on a standard research laptop.
These times are generally longer than comparable Mplus runs on the same data, and will scale with sample size, number of time points, and model complexity.
Several strategies can reduce Stan runtimes in practice.

The most immediate is within-chain parallelization via the reduce_sum function in Stan, combined with CmdStanR's parallel_chains and threads_per_chain arguments, which distribute chains and within-chain computations across available cores (Gabry et al., 2025; Stan Development Team, 2022).

For large datasets or models that need to be run repeatedly, for example across a simulation study or in a tutorial setting with multiple model variants, an RDS-based caching workflow in R can also avoid redundant refitting.

While Stan will not always be faster than Mplus in absolute terms, the richer convergence diagnostics it provides mean that researchers can be more confident that the time invested in sampling has produced trustworthy posterior estimates.

The approach presented in this tutorial assumes that observations are equally spaced in time, which is common in cognitive task and laboratory paradigms but is not always the case in ambulatory assessment or daily diary designs.

When measurement occasions are unequally spaced, the autoregressive parameter ϕ no longer has a constant interpretation across adjacent pairs of observations, because the strength of temporal carry-over decays as a function of the elapsed time between measurements.
As Berkhout et al. (2025) note, in an AR(1) process with ϕ = 0.3, the implied association between observations two steps apart is ϕ2 = 0.09, and the decay is exponential as the interval grows.
text.formatted: As <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Berkhout et al. (2025)</ref> note, in an AR(1) process with ϕ = 0.3, the implied association between observations two steps apart is ϕ2 = 0.09, and the decay is exponential as the interval grows.

text.text: The choice of measurement interval therefore has direct consequences for parameter estimation and interpretation (Deboeck & Preacher, 2016; Dormann & Griffin, 2015; Reichardt, 2011).

text.text: Mplus addresses this through the TINTERVAL option, which inserts placeholder observations at regular time intervals so that the lag structure remains constant and interpretable.

Our Stan implementation handles the same problem in a conceptually equivalent but more explicit way: rather than automated insertion by the software, the researcher prepares the data in R by marking the positions of missing observations with
Inf values and passing their indices to Stan as part of the data list.
Stan then estimates the values at those positions as unknown parameters, informed by the surrounding observations and the dynamic structure of the model.

The key difference is one of transparency and control: the researcher decides where to insert missing observations and can verify that the temporal structure passed to Stan matches their intentions, rather than relying on software-automated restructuring.

The substantive modeling challenge identified by Asparouhov et al. (2018), namely that the chosen time unit should be interpretable, should not generate excessive missingness, and should preserve the original time metric, applies equally to both approaches.

text.text: A further extension that falls outside the scope of this tutorial is three-level DSEM, in which observations are nested within days or sessions, which are themselves nested within persons.
This structure arises naturally in ambulatory assessment designs with multiple beeps per day, and in cognitive paradigms where trial-level data are collected across multiple testing sessions.
Very recently Mplus released Version 9 with a native three-level DSEM estimator (Asparouhov & Muthén, 2025).

text.text: In principle, three-level DSEM can also be implemented in Stan, because it only requires adding a further level of random effects to the model code presented here.
Developing and evaluating such an implementation is, however, a task for future research.

This paper set out to lower the barrier to implementing Dynamic Structural Equation Models in Stan by providing a step-by-step tutorial that builds from a minimal model to a fully reparameterized implementation with Bayesian missing data handling, and then extends to two model classes, residual DSEM and categorical predictor variables, that are not currently available in other R packages using stan.

The reparameterization strategy demonstrated here, switching from a centered to a non-centered parameterization of the random effects, resolved the convergence difficulties encountered in the simpler model and proved robust even when random effect variance components were near zero, a setting where the centered parameterization in mlts required additional constraints.

The Bayesian data augmentation approach to missing values made the imputation model explicit and directly consistent with the substantive model, with uncertainty about missing observations propagating naturally through the posterior.

We hope that the modular structure of the code presented here makes it straightforward for researchers to adapt the models to their own research questions, whether by adding between-level predictors, extending to three levels, incorporating measurement error via latent variables, or combining features from the RDSEM and categorical extensions demonstrated here.

The fundamental skills involved, writing Stan data, parameter, and model blocks, reparameterizing for faster, more reliable sampling, and handling missing data as parameters, transfer directly to a wide range of models beyond those covered in this tutorial.

Following the recommendations ofSchubert et al. (2025) for reporting Bayesian analyses, a complete DSEM report should contain four elements.
text.formatted: Following the recommendations of<ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Schubert et al. (2025)</ref> for reporting Bayesian analyses, a complete DSEM report should contain four elements.

text.text: First, it should state the distribution, parameter values, and a brief rationale for every prior, with each prior scaled to the parameter it governs (see the The model Block section).
Second, it should describe the estimation setup: the software and package versions, the number of chains, the number of warm-up and post-warm-up iterations, and the random seed.

Third, it should report the convergence and sampler diagnostics introduced in the Convergence section for all parameters, together with any remedial steps taken when the initial diagnostics were unsatisfactory.
In this tutorial, the switch from the centered to the non-centered parameterization is one such step, and it belongs in the report rather than being hidden.
Fourth, it should summarize the results with posterior medians and credible intervals, stating the interval type.
The cmdstanr default used here is the equal-tailed quantile interval, which can differ from a highest-density interval for skewed posteriors such as variance components.

Conclusions should be framed in terms of the magnitude of an effect and the uncertainty around it rather than in frequentist language; describing an effect as "significant" or only asking whether a credible interval excludes zero discards much of the information a posterior provides.

The first is a list of what each outcome still has to explain at occasion t (its centered value minus the autoregressive prediction).
The second holds the person-specific effects of MI * on each outcome, and the third the person-specific residual standard deviations (note: standard deviations, not variances).

The fourth is the person's cutpoint: the threshold minus the person's MI propensity, so that a person with a high propensity needs a smaller push on Appendix A Preparing the Data in R This appendix shows how the data are prepared in R before they are passed to Stan (see the Implementation in Stan: Simplest Model section).

text.text: The file defines a new distribution, categorical_predictor(), that takes care of all the mathematics needed when a binary variable is used as a within-level predictor of one or more continuous outcomes.
Moving this code into its own file keeps the categorical model as close as possible to the full model: only a few lines change in the main model, and the helper itself never needs to be edited.

To use it, place the file in the same folder as your model file and add the following lines at the top of the model (see the section on includes in Stan Development Team, 2022): functions { # include d s e m _ c a t e g o r i c a l _ h e l p e r . stan } [i , t ] ∼ c a t e g o r i c a l _ p r e d i c t o r ( resid , beta , psi , cutpoint );Here, C[i,t] is the observed binary variable (1, 0, or any negative number for missing); resid holds, for each continuous outcome, the person-centered value at time t minus everything the model predicts for it apart from the effect of the latent variable C * (so minus the autoregressive term and any further covariates); beta holds the person's regression coefficients of each outcome on C * ; psi holds the person's residual standard deviations; and cutpoint is the probit threshold minus the person's propensity for C.Because resid, beta, and psi are lists, the same file serves a DSEM with one outcome or with ten.
) If C it is missing, nothing is added.
The occasion then still contributes the probability of the outcomes from Step 3.

This is important: it means that missing values of the continuous outcomes at such occasions are still imputed based on the model, rather than drifting freely. if ( C == 1) { lp += log_Phi_stable ( -( cutpoint -m ) / sqrt ( v )); // C * above the cutpoint } else if ( C == 0) { lp += log_Phi_stable (( cutpoint -m ) / sqrt ( v )); // C * below the cutpoint } Because the function is named with the suffix _lpmf (log probability mass function) in the helper file, Stan allows it to be used with the familiar tilde (~) notation in the model, just like built-in distributions such as normal() (Stan Development Team, 2022).
